I have been contacted by a couple of (nice) people in leading roles in other cryptos' foundations. And the question is usually: why #Doge, and why not our coin, that we think is more technically sound?

I usually answer: because #Dogecoin has a dog in it; your coin does not.

I know many who bought #Dogecoin at the peak in January 2018 (around 0.02 USD). Within a few months the price collapsed to 1/10th the value.

Those people had to wait until 2021 to sell at a profit.

But be careful: even this consideration is not a guarantee of anything.

And this is why we keep repeating: buy small amounts at a time; do not play with leverage, ever; do not bet house money, farm money, student loans, or family savings.

Put into crypto only money you can afford to lose or to have locked into an asset long term. #dogecoin

Your #Dogecoin and other crypto becomes real only when you withdraw it to your private wallet. At that point your holdings go on-chain, and you finally hold in your wallet "real" Dogecoin.

Remember: exchanges are for trading, not for holding.

When you buy #Dogecoin or any crypto from an exchange, your holdings are living within a virtual ledger/database internal to the exchange and opaque to the outside: they could be just IOUs, made-up numbers. The exchange could be selling more than what they hold in their wallets.

To clarify another source of confusion.

BSC-Doge being backed by collateral does not say anything about how fractional the reserve backing users' holdings on the exchange is: these are two completely different things. 

#Dogecoin

Anyhow, this does NOT mean that you should ever hold Doge long term as BSC-Doge. Any wrapped token should in general be used only for interoperability  - in other words, to use #Dogecoin on another network, possibly for a short time.
